title: Inguinal + popliteal lymphadenopathy: lateral foot lesion (lateral lymphatic track)
vignette: A 48-year-old man comes to the office due to right inguinal discomfort. The patient first noticed "bumps" in his groin when he was dressing in the morning. He does not know how long they have been present but thinks they are relatively new. The patient was treated for gonorrhea several years ago but has no other medical problems. He drinks alcohol occasionally but does not use tobacco or illicit drugs. His mother died of metastatic melanoma. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. The abdomen is soft and nontender. The right inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged and tender, as are several nodes in the right popliteal area. The distribution of lymphadenopathy in this patient would most likely be seen in which of the following conditions?

clues.text: right inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged and tender
clues.note: The superficial inguinal nodes receive lymph from most of the lower extremity, perineum, and lower abdominal wall - so many sources cause inguinal adenopathy.

clues.text: several nodes in the right popliteal area
clues.note: POPLITEAL node involvement is the key discriminator: it indicates drainage via the LATERAL lymphatic track (lateral foot/leg), which reaches the popliteal nodes before the inguinal nodes.

whatMatters: The lower limb has a MEDIAL track (great toe/medial foot -> straight to inguinal nodes, BYPASSING popliteal) and a LATERAL track (lateral foot -> POPLITEAL nodes -> inguinal nodes). Involvement of BOTH popliteal AND inguinal nodes points to a LATERAL foot lesion. Answer D (purulent laceration on the right lateral foot).
strategy: Use the popliteal nodes as the discriminator. Lateral foot/leg lesions drain via the LATERAL track through the POPLITEAL nodes then to inguinal - explaining BOTH sets. Reject the great-toe melanoma (medial track -> inguinal only, bypasses popliteal), and the pelvic/genital sources: prostate (internal iliac nodes), testicular mass (para-aortic nodes), and glans penis (deep inguinal nodes) - none involve popliteal nodes.

options.text: Large, irregular mole on the right great toe
Purulent laceration on the right lateral foot
Ulcerative lesion on the glans penis

eliminations.label: Prostate nodules - internal iliac nodes
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: prostate pathology (hard nodules). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the prostate drains primarily to the INTERNAL ILIAC nodes, not inguinal or popliteal. ✅ Correct if: pelvic (internal iliac) lymphadenopathy.

eliminations.label: Testicular mass - para-aortic nodes
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a testicular tumor. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the testes drain to PARA-AORTIC (retroperitoneal) nodes (following gonadal vessels), not to inguinal/popliteal nodes. ✅ Correct if: retroperitoneal (para-aortic) adenopathy. Note the SCROTUM drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

eliminations.label: Great-toe melanoma - inguinal only (bypasses popliteal)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a lesion on the medial foot/great toe (worrisome given family melanoma). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the MEDIAL track drains straight to the SUPERFICIAL INGUINAL nodes, BYPASSING the popliteal nodes - so it wouldn't cause popliteal adenopathy. ✅ Correct if: isolated inguinal (no popliteal) lymphadenopathy.

eliminations.label: Glans penis lesion - deep inguinal nodes
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an ulcer on the glans penis. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the glans drains mainly via the DEEP inguinal (and iliac) nodes and does not involve the popliteal nodes. ✅ Correct if: deep inguinal/iliac adenopathy (glans/penile urethra).

reasoning: Popliteal node involvement indicates drainage through the lateral lymphatic track
The lateral track carries lymph from the lateral foot/leg to popliteal then inguinal nodes
A lateral foot lesion therefore causes BOTH popliteal and inguinal adenopathy
-> purulent laceration on the right lateral foot; answer D
mechanism: The lymphatic drainage of the lower extremity has SUPERFICIAL vessels (following the veins) organized into two tracks. The MEDIAL track runs along the great saphenous vein from the MEDIAL foot/leg directly to the SUPERFICIAL INGUINAL nodes, BYPASSING the popliteal nodes. The LATERAL track drains the LATERAL foot/leg to the POPLITEAL nodes first, which then relay to the inguinal nodes. Consequently, lesions of the MEDIAL foot (e.g., a great-toe melanoma) cause inguinal adenopathy WITHOUT popliteal involvement, whereas LATERAL foot/leg lesions cause BOTH popliteal AND inguinal adenopathy. This patient has enlarged inguinal AND popliteal nodes, so a LATERAL foot source (a purulent laceration) best fits. The distractors drain elsewhere: prostate -> internal iliac; testis -> para-aortic; glans penis -> deep inguinal/iliac - none reach the popliteal nodes.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Anatomy > lower-limb lymphatics: medial track (great saphenous) -> superficial inguinal (bypasses popliteal); lateral track -> popliteal -> inguinal; genital drainage - scrotum to superficial inguinal, testis to para-aortic, glans to deep inguinal.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Popliteal + inguinal nodes = lateral foot lesion (lateral track); medial foot = inguinal only.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on superficial inguinal vs popliteal nodes, medial/lateral lymphatic tracks, or para-aortic drainage? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Great toe = medial track (inguinal only); prostate = internal iliac; testis = para-aortic; glans = deep inguinal.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: lateral foot -> popliteal + inguinal; medial foot/great toe -> inguinal only (bypasses popliteal).

firstAid.detail: Anatomy: lateral track -> popliteal -> inguinal; medial -> inguinal only.
Anatomy > testis para-aortic, scrotum inguinal, glans deep inguinal, prostate internal iliac.
Onc > sentinel node basins follow these tracks.

memoryHook: Popliteal nodes are the tollbooth on the LATERAL road; light them up and the lesion is on the outer foot - the medial road (great toe) skips straight to the groin.
